newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Miller demand increases in Brazil amid high prices.
newsitem.headline: Miller demand increases in Brazil amid high prices.

text.p: Millers are buying increasing quantities of Brazilian wheat at the government's regular auctions, spurred by higher subsidies and a rise in international prices, analysts and millers said.

The government sold 67,650 tonnes of the 160,000 tonnes it offered at the most recent auction on January 10. The average subsidy was around 33 reais ($31.7), said a spokesman for Banco do Brasil which handles the auctions.
On average, around 45 percent of the amount offered has been sold in the three auctions held since the start of the year. This compares with some 30 percent in mid-December.

"It's a combination of higher subsidies and the firmness of Argentine prices," said Gil Barabach, analyst at independent consultants Safras e Mercado. "Prices firmed more than the domestic industry was expecting."

Prices on the Chicago wheat market have been underpinned by fears of winterkill in the U.S. Midwest and shot up on Friday after the USDA's estimate of 1997 U.S. planted area came in sharply lower than expected.

Meanwhile, Argentine wheat rose after widespread rains hit crops in December, affecting both output and quality. Latest prices quoted Argentine wheat offered at $150 free-on-board (FOB) compared to around $130 last month.
"Brazilian wheat offered at state auctions is cheaper than Argentine wheat at this stage," said Lawrence Pih, president of Moinho Pacifico.
In auctions millers bid for wheat not at an outright price but at a subsidy to the minimum price of 157 reais ($152).
The miller pays the government the minimum price minus the subsidy set at the auction while the government pays the farmer the full minimum price.
The advantage for the government is that it does not have to pay for the storage of wheat as in previous years, with the wheat passing directly from the farmer to the mill.
The subsidy ranged from 16 reais ($15.4) in Parana to 34 reais ($32.6) in Rio Grande do Sul and 69 reais ($66.3) in the north of the country, according to Pih.

"I would be very happy to pay the prices currently quoted for higher quality wheat from the north of Parana, but this is virtually disappearing," said Pih. "In the west of Parana there is more available but it is of lower quality."
Barabach said that cooperatives and traders were offering the higher quality wheat outside of government auctions at 162 to 165 reais ($156-159).

"There is some high quality wheat available in the north of Parana that they would never want to sell through the government auctions, but it's a very small amount," he said. "In the internal market, the big problem is the lack of quality."
Demand for wheat from Argentina, traditionally Brazil's biggest supplier, should remain strong as most millers were using domestic wheat to mix with higher quality produce.
Safras estimated that Brazil imported a total of 5.75 million tonnes of wheat in the 1996/97 harvest year, with Argentina accounting for some 4.5 to five million tonnes.
Some analysts thought that demand at coming Brazilian state auctions could drop off as the quality of the wheat offered declined, adding that freight costs in some areas were high.
The government is estimated to have some 700,000 tonnes of wheat still available for sale, meaning that at the current pace of sales it should exhaust its stocks by March.
"I think the auctions will go on until April," said Pih. "As the quality deteriorates, there may not be much interest left."
The main buyers were usually larger mills, who bought from 5,000 to 20,000 or 30,000 tonnes.

Barabach forecast the high level of subsidies, which rose from an average of 16 reais ($15.4) in mid-December, would keep demand firm at between 60,000 and 70,000 tonnes per auction. This meant the auctions should end in late February-early March.
